subject: chemistry
title: Measurement & Data Processing Adventure 1: Errors and uncertainties
welcome_lead: Today you'll quantify random and systematic errors in your data.
meta_desc: Chemistry — random vs systematic errors, absolute and percentage uncertainty, propagation.
final_note: You learned random errors scatter results, systematic errors shift mean; uncertainties propagate by adding absolutes (+/-) or percentages (×/÷).

walkthroughs.body_html:
Random: scatter from human reading, fluctuations. Mean of many trials helps.

Systematic: same direction every time (e.g. uncalibrated balance, parallax, heat loss). Mean does not help — must fix cause.

Precision ≠ accuracy: a stuck stopwatch is precise but inaccurate.

Each instrument has minimum uncertainty:
- Burette: ± 0.05 cm³
- Pipette: ± 0.05 cm³
- Balance: ± 0.005 g
- Thermometer: ± 0.5°C

% uncertainty = (absolute / value) × 100.
For 25.00 cm³ ± 0.05: 0.05/25 × 100 = 0.2%.

- Adding/subtracting: add absolutes.
- Multiplying/dividing: add percentages.
- Power: multiply % by power.

Example: titration. Vol acid 25.00 ± 0.10, vol base 22.50 ± 0.10.
If divided, % uncertainties: 0.4% + 0.44% = 0.84%.

Report final answer to same number of sig figs as smallest uncertainty allows.

mcqs.q: What are the units of Kc for a reaction?
options: Kc always has units of mol dm^-3.
They depend on Δn (the difference between moles of gaseous/aqueous products and reactants) — Kc can be dimensionless or have units like mol dm^-3.
A reaction with negative delta G must be exothermic in every case.

mcqs.q: If a reaction has a negative Gibbs free energy change, what does that mean?
options: A reaction with negative delta G must be exothermic in every case.
The reaction is thermodynamically feasible — it can proceed — but it may still be very slow.
A reaction with negative delta G will always happen quickly.

mcqs.q: Can a single standard electrode potential be measured in isolation?
options: Each electrode has an absolute potential that can be measured directly with a voltmeter.
Standard electrode potentials are measured by submerging the electrode in pure water.
No — electrode potentials are RELATIVE values measured against a reference (the standard hydrogen electrode, defined as 0 V).
A reaction with negative delta G must be exothermic in every case.
